title: Repositories, Contributors, and Continuity: An Empirical Study of Foundational Quantum Software
authors: Vincent Gierisch, Nicole Hoess, Ralf Ramsauer, Wolfgang Mauerer
abstract: Driven by contributions from academia, industry, and open-source communities, the quantum software ecosystem is rapidly growing. Across this ecosystem, new concepts often emerge through software artefacts accompanying scientific publications as well as through sustained development in larger communities. However, many repositories receive development efforts only over a limited period of time, raising the question whether their concepts persist beyond individual repositories. In this paper, we apply established empirical software engineering techniques to analyse a set of foundational quantum software repositories. We combine cross-repository activity with contributor relationships to study the evolution of communities. Our analysis provides empirical evidence of contributor migration patterns and indications of cross-project knowledge transfer. We observe multiple development paths: projects may evolve into sustained communities, contributors may integrate concepts into established ecosystems, or activity may continue through new and follow-up software artefacts. Our observations provide an initial empirical perspective on how concepts and influence persist across repository boundaries in quantum software ecosystems.
summary: This paper empirically analyzes the structure of the quantum software ecosystem by tracking developer contributions across multiple foundational repositories. Using software engineering techniques, it maps out how expertise flows between projects over time. The findings demonstrate that knowledge transfer is a key feature of this rapidly growing field, suggesting concepts persist even when individual project activity wanes.
main_problem: The study investigates whether scientific concepts and development influence persist across the boundaries of individual software repositories within the rapidly expanding quantum software ecosystem.
main_result: Knowledge transfer is evident through developer migration patterns, suggesting that expertise often moves across repository boundaries rather than being confined to a single project.
method: The authors applied empirical software engineering techniques by analyzing Git commit data and cross-repository contributions to map community evolution.
model_or_system: The system analyzed is the quantum software ecosystem itself, modeled as a network of interconnected repositories (projects) and developers who contribute code across them.
key_observables: Contributor migration patterns, cross-project knowledge transfer indications, developer roles (Exclusive vs. Cross-Project; Core vs. Peripheral), and temporal contribution activity.
important_parameters: Commit count per developer/project/day, time elapsed between contributions in different projects.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that knowledge transfer occurs primarily through the direct, measurable activity of individual developers moving between projects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the workflow from publications to repository mapping, show the overall ecosystem network linking developers and projects, and display contribution activity over time tracing top contributors across multiple repositories.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure involving defining the problem (concept persistence), detailing the multi-stage MSR pipeline (selection $ightarrow$ extraction $ightarrow$ mapping $ightarrow$ networking $ightarrow$ temporal analysis), presenting empirical evidence of developer roles and migration, and concluding with observed development paths.
why_interesting: While not directly focused on physical models, understanding the infrastructure and community dynamics supporting quantum software is crucial for any theoretical physicist needing to implement or test complex algorithms in practice.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the analysis workflow. We first relate quantum software repositories to associated publications and derive repository-level observations from the development history. We then map contributor identities across repositories and construct complementary ecosystem and temporal views to capture relations and evolution beyond individual projects. This allows for analysing activity, contributor dynamics, and the continuation of concepts in the ecosystem.

Fig. 2. Overview of the quantum software ecosystem with projects (grey nodes) and contributors (blue nodes and edges for developers contributing to multiple projects; lilac nodes and edges for developers contributing to a single project). Developer nodes are scaled by their total commits across the entire ecosystem. Edge widths indicate the share of commits (effort) a developer contributed to the specific project during their active months.

Fig. 3. Contribution activity over time. Violins show the overall commit distribution per project. Coloured points mark the top 20% (24 of 118 cross-project) contributors by total commits. Each of the colour–shape combinations denotes a single developer, allowing the same contributor to be traced across projects.
